hints: Start by looking at Fig. 2.1 and tracing where the blood is at all times - is it ever free in body spaces or is it always inside tubes?
Now count how many times blood going round the whole body must go through the heart, thinking about the separate loop to the lungs and the loop to the rest of the body.
walkthrough:
Why Closed - Blood Stays Inside Vessels**
Think of the blood as staying in pipes all the time. In humans blood never bathes the tissues directly. It stays inside arteries, capillaries and veins, and only plasma and small solutes leak out to form tissue fluid. That containment is what closed means.

Why Double - Two Circuits Through the Heart**
Follow one red blood cell round Fig. 2.1. From the heart it goes to the lungs, back to the heart, then out to the head, liver, kidneys and legs, then back to the heart again. So for one full tour it passes the heart twice - once for the pulmonary circulation to the lungs and once for the systemic circulation to the body.
Final answer: closed because blood is contained within blood vessels; double because blood flows through the heart twice for one complete circuit of the body.

hints: Follow the arrows in Fig. 2.1 - remember Q is bringing blood back up to the right side of the heart and R is taking blood away from the left side to the head and arms.
walkthrough:
Reading Flow Arrows to Name Q and R**
Look at the direction of the white arrows. Q has blood flowing upwards into the right side of the heart from the lower body, so it is the large vein returning deoxygenated blood, the vena cava. R has blood flowing away from the left side of the heart up toward the head and arms, so it is the main large artery leaving the heart, the aorta.
Final answer: Q = vena cava and R = aorta.

hints: Recall from (a)(ii) which vessel is the vein and which is the artery, then think about the very different blood pressures they have to cope with.
Picture a cross-section of each wall - focus on overall wall thickness, size of the lumen, and the middle muscle and elastic layer.
Link low pressure in Q to needing less muscle and elastic tissue compared with the high pressure vessel R, without mentioning valves.
walkthrough:
Q Is Low Pressure, R Is High Pressure**
Q is the vena cava, a vein carrying blood at low pressure back to the heart. R is the aorta, an artery receiving blood pumped at very high pressure from the left ventricle. Wall structure follows that pressure difference.

Wall, Lumen and Tunica Media Differences**
Because of low pressure, Q has a much thinner overall wall and a thinner tunica media, the middle layer. Its lumen is wide relative to that thin wall, giving a floppy tube, while R has a thick wall and a relatively narrower lumen to withstand and maintain pressure.

Muscle and Elastic Tissue**
R needs lots of smooth muscle to constrict and lots of elastic fibres to stretch and recoil with each pulse. Q needs proportionately much less smooth muscle and very few elastic fibres because it does not have to stretch under pressure or help push blood by vasoconstriction to the same extent.
Final answer: Q (vein) has: thinner wall than R; wider lumen relative to wall thickness; thinner tunica media; proportionately less smooth muscle; proportionately less / very few elastic fibres.

hints: Count the separate polypeptide strands you can see in the shark antibody in Fig. 2.2, then recall the standard Y-shaped human antibody with its paired short and long chains.
walkthrough:
Counting Chains - Shark Versus Human**
Quaternary structure means how many separate polypeptide chains are put together. Fig. 2.2 shows the shark antibody made of only two chains joined together. The normal human antibody is bigger, built from four polypeptides together - two identical short light chains on the arms and two identical longer heavy chains forming the stem and core of the Y.
Final answer: Human antibodies are made of four polypeptides / contain two light chains and two heavy chains.

hints: Think about the journey an antibody must make from blood plasma to a tumour cell - what barrier must it cross to leave the capillary and get into the tissue fluid?
Now link smaller size to getting through that barrier in larger numbers and reaching more hidden cancer cells, and what that means for destroying the tumour.
walkthrough:
Leaving the Blood to Reach the Tumour**
To attack a tumour, antibodies in the plasma must escape the capillary through small gaps between endothelial cells into the tissue fluid, then diffuse through the tumour mass. Large human antibodies struggle to get out and penetrate far, so only a small percentage reach inner cancer cells.

Why Smaller Is More Effective**
Smaller shark antibodies slip through those endothelial gaps more easily, so more of them enter the tissue fluid around the tumour. They can also diffuse further through the tightly packed tumour to bind antigens on more cancer cells, so more cells are marked for destruction quickly. Their small size may also make them less likely to trigger an unwanted immune response.

Final answer: More pass through gaps in capillary wall / endothelium; so more enter tissue fluid surrounding tumour cells; more cancer cells destroyed quickly / diffuse more easily through tumour to reach more cells.

hints: Think about what type of immunity you get when you are given ready-made antibodies rather than making them yourself, and how fast that works.
Picture what the Y-shaped tips of those injected antibodies will attach to on the invading pathogen or its toxins.
Now link that binding to how it helps phagocytes find and destroy the pathogen, for example by clumping or coating it.
walkthrough:
Ready-Made Protection - Artificial Passive Immunity**
Injecting antibodies gives artificial passive immunity. It is artificial because the antibodies come from outside, and passive because the person does not make their own memory cells. The big advantage is speed - protection is immediate with no wait for B-cell activation and plasma cell production.

Binding Antigen and Toxin**
The variable regions of the injected antibodies bind specifically to non-self antigens on the surface of the pathogen. If the pathogen releases toxins, antibodies also bind and neutralise them, acting as antitoxins so they cannot damage body cells.

Helping Phagocytes Clear the Pathogen**
Coating the pathogen acts as opsonisation, marking it clearly for phagocytes to engulf by phagocytosis. Antibodies can also cross-link pathogens causing agglutination or clumping, and immobilise them by binding flagella, making them much easier for phagocytes to destroy before disease develops.

Final answer: Gives artificial passive immunity; fast acting as no time needed for immune response; antibody binds to foreign antigen on pathogen surface; antibodies neutralise toxins / act as antitoxins; promotes phagocytosis by opsonisation / agglutination.
